summary: How a single heart tube folds, loops, and divides into four chambers with valves and outflow vessels, and how fetal circulation bypasses the lungs and liver. Exam questions link each embryonic structure to its adult derivative and to the congenital defect that results when a step fails.

points: Heart forms from splanchnic mesoderm (cardiogenic field) in week 3.
Paired endocardial tubes fuse into one heart tube as the embryo folds.
Heart beats spontaneously by about day 22 (week 4); first functional organ.
Looping begins in week 4 and sets left-right position of the chambers.
Defective left-right dynein (primary ciliary dyskinesia, Kartagener syndrome) can cause dextrocardia with situs inversus.
Septum primum grows toward the endocardial cushions; the gap below it is the ostium primum.
Ostium secundum opens by apoptosis in the upper septum primum.
Septum secundum grows on the right side of septum primum and leaves an opening, the foramen ovale.
Septum primum acts as a one-way flap valve over the foramen ovale.
After birth, left atrial pressure rises above right and presses the flap shut; the scar is the fossa ovalis.
Failure of the two septa to fuse leaves a patent foramen ovale (about 1 in 4 adults).

notes.h: Ventricles, AV canal, and outflow tract
points: Dorsal and ventral endocardial cushions fuse to split the AV canal into right and left channels.
Muscular interventricular septum grows up from the floor of the ventricle.
Membranous septum closes the last gap using endocardial cushion and outflow ridge tissue; most VSDs are membranous.
Neural crest cells form truncal and bulbar ridges that spiral to make the aorticopulmonary septum.
Mitral and tricuspid valves come from fused AV canal endocardial cushions; aortic and pulmonary valves come from outflow tract endocardial cushions.
Umbilical vein carries the most oxygenated fetal blood from the placenta.
Ductus venosus lets most umbilical blood bypass the liver into the IVC.
IVC blood is directed through the foramen ovale to the left atrium, then to the head and upper body.
SVC blood goes RA to RV to pulmonary trunk, then through the ductus arteriosus to the descending aorta.
High fetal pulmonary vascular resistance drives the ductus shunt.
Two umbilical arteries (from the internal iliac arteries) return deoxygenated blood to the placenta.
First breaths drop pulmonary vascular resistance, so more blood returns to the left atrium.
Higher left atrial pressure closes the foramen ovale.
Rising O2 and falling prostaglandin E2 (placenta removed) constrict the ductus arteriosus.
Clamping the cord stops flow in the umbilical vessels and ductus venosus.

Shunts pulmonary trunk blood to the aorta

tricks.label: 1st arch is MAXimal, Second = Stapedial, C is the 3rd letter, 4 limbs = systemic, 6th = pulmonary
tricks.text: Arch 1: maxillary artery. Arch 2: stapedial artery. Arch 3: common carotid. Arch 4: systemic vessels (aortic arch, right subclavian). Arch 6: pulmonary arteries and the pulmonary-to-systemic shunt (ductus arteriosus).

tricks.label: The 5 Ts of early cyanosis
tricks.text: Truncus arteriosus, Transposition of the great arteries, Tricuspid atresia, Tetralogy of Fallot, TAPVR. The first, second, and fourth are outflow tract (neural crest) septation errors.

tricks.label: Follow the oxygen
tricks.text: Trace one red cell from the placenta: umbilical vein, ductus venosus, IVC, foramen ovale, LA, LV, aorta to the brain. Every shunt exists to send the best blood to the brain and skip the airless lungs and busy liver.

highYield: Neural crest failure in the outflow tract gives persistent truncus arteriosus, transposition, or tetralogy of Fallot.
22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge) is linked to truncus arteriosus and tetralogy of Fallot.
Endocardial cushion defects (AV septal defect) are classic in Down syndrome.
Patent foramen ovale can let a venous clot cross to the systemic side (paradoxical embolism).
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the ligamentum arteriosum (6th arch) and aortic arch; the right hooks under the right subclavian artery (4th arch).
Most VSDs are in the membranous septum.
pitfalls: Ligamentum venosum comes from the ductus venosus; ligamentum arteriosum comes from the ductus arteriosus.
Medial umbilical ligaments are old umbilical arteries; the median umbilical ligament is the urachus (allantois), which is not a vessel.
Ostium secundum forms in septum primum; the foramen ovale is the hole left in septum secundum.
Failure to form the aorticopulmonary septum gives truncus arteriosus; failure of the septum to spiral gives transposition.

Ductus venosus bypasses the liver to the IVC (ligamentum venosum)
Foramen ovale moves blood RA to LA (fossa ovalis)
Ductus arteriosus moves blood pulmonary trunk to aorta (ligamentum arteriosum)
High pulmonary vascular resistance explains why lungs are bypassed
Two umbilical arteries from internal iliacs return blood (medial umbilical ligaments)
Umbilical vein becomes ligamentum teres hepatis

summary: The microscopic structure of the heart wall, cardiac muscle cells, and the different types of blood vessels. Questions ask you to match a wall feature to its function and to know which layer is affected in common vascular diseases.

points: Endocardium: endothelium plus thin connective tissue; the subendocardial layer holds Purkinje fibers, nerves, and small vessels.
Myocardium: thickest layer, made of cardiac muscle cells; thickest in the left ventricle.
Epicardium: visceral layer of serous pericardium (mesothelium) over fat that carries the coronary vessels.
Cardiac skeleton: dense connective tissue rings around the valves; electrically insulates atria from ventricles except at the AV bundle.
Valve leaflets: dense connective tissue core covered by endothelium on both sides.
Striated, branched cells with one or two central nuclei.
Intercalated discs join cells end to end: fascia adherens and desmosomes hold, gap junctions pass current.
Gap junctions let the heart contract as a functional syncytium.
T tubules sit at the Z lines and pair with one SR cistern (diads).
Very rich in mitochondria; the heart depends on aerobic metabolism.
Atrial muscle cells contain granules of atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP).
Adult cardiac muscle barely regenerates; dead muscle is replaced by fibrous scar.
Larger and paler than working myocytes, with fewer myofibrils and lots of glycogen.
Lie in the subendocardium and conduct impulses fast.
Tunica intima: endothelium, basal lamina, subendothelial connective tissue; arteries add an internal elastic lamina.
Tunica media: smooth muscle and elastic tissue; thickest layer in arteries.
Tunica adventitia: collagen-rich connective tissue; thickest layer in large veins.
Vasa vasorum supply the outer wall of large vessels and are more plentiful in veins.
Limb veins have valves (folds of intima) that stop backflow.
Nitric oxide and prostacyclin relax smooth muscle and resist clotting.
Endothelin-1 is a strong vasoconstrictor.
Weibel-Palade bodies store von Willebrand factor and P-selectin.

rows: Gap junctions in single-unit smooth muscle

tricks.label: Arteries flex, veins hold
tricks.text: Arteries face high pressure, so their media is thick. Veins hold volume at low pressure, so their adventitia is the thickest layer and the lumen is wide.

tricks.label: Leakiness matches the job
tricks.text: Where cells and large proteins must pass (liver, spleen, marrow) capillaries are sinusoidal. Where filtration or hormone release happens (kidney, gut, endocrine) they are fenestrated. Everywhere else they are continuous.

tricks.label: Disc parts by direction
tricks.text: In an intercalated disc, the parts that run across the cell end (fascia adherens, desmosomes) hold cells together; the parts along the side (gap junctions) carry the electrical signal.

highYield: Gap junctions in intercalated discs make the myocardium a functional syncytium.
Infarcted myocardium heals by fibrous scar because cardiac muscle cells barely divide.
Arterioles set most of the systemic vascular resistance.
Postcapillary venules are where neutrophils leave the blood in acute inflammation.
Continuous capillaries with tight junctions form the blood-brain barrier.
Atherosclerosis starts in the intima; Monckeberg medial calcific sclerosis affects the media of muscular arteries.
pitfalls: Cardiac T tubules sit at Z lines (diads); skeletal T tubules sit at A-I junctions (triads).
Purkinje fibers are larger and paler than working myocytes; their wide diameter helps them conduct fast.
The epicardium is the same thing as the visceral serous pericardium.
In arteries the media is the thickest layer; in large veins the adventitia is.

summary: Where the heart sits in the chest, which chambers form each surface and border, how the great vessels connect, and how the pericardium wraps it all. Exam questions use these relations to explain stab wounds, enlarged chambers, referred pain, and tamponade.

points: Heart lies in the middle mediastinum inside the pericardium, about two thirds left of midline.
Apex sits behind the left 5th intercostal space at about the midclavicular line.
The plane through the sternal angle and the T4/T5 disc separates superior from inferior mediastinum.
Right ventricle is the most anterior chamber, right behind the sternum.
Left atrium is the most posterior chamber, right in front of the esophagus.
Fibrous pericardium: tough outer sac fused to the central tendon of the diaphragm and to the adventitia of the great vessels.
Serous pericardium has a parietal layer (lines the fibrous sac) and a visceral layer (epicardium).
Pericardial cavity holds a thin film of serous fluid between the two serous layers.
Phrenic nerves (C3 to C5) carry pain from the fibrous and parietal layers; pain refers to the shoulder and supraclavicular skin.
Main blood supply is the pericardiacophrenic artery from the internal thoracic artery.
Transverse pericardial sinus lies behind the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk, in front of the SVC.
Oblique pericardial sinus is a blind pouch behind the left atrium, bounded by the pulmonary veins and IVC.
SVC (formed by the two brachiocephalic veins) and IVC enter the right atrium; the azygos vein drains into the SVC.
Pulmonary trunk leaves the RV and divides into right and left pulmonary arteries under the aortic arch.
Usually four pulmonary veins enter the left atrium.
The coronary arteries are the only branches of the ascending aorta.
Aortic arch branches, right to left: brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian.
Ligamentum arteriosum links the left pulmonary artery to the underside of the arch; the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the arch next to it.
RA: crista terminalis separates smooth sinus venarum from pectinate muscle; fossa ovalis on the septum; coronary sinus opening.
RV: trabeculae carneae, three papillary muscles, smooth conus arteriosus leading to the pulmonary valve.
Moderator band (septomarginal trabecula) carries part of the right bundle branch to the anterior papillary muscle.
LV wall is about two to three times thicker than the RV wall; two papillary muscles (anterior and posterior).

charts.title: Heart chambers at a glance
rows: Crista terminalis, pectinate muscles, fossa ovalis, SA node near SVC opening
Trabeculae carneae, moderator band, three papillary muscles, conus arteriosus
Mostly smooth wall; pectinate muscles only in left auricle
Thickest wall, two papillary muscles, smooth aortic vestibule

charts.title: Which chamber forms each surface and border
rows: Left atrium, small part of right atrium
Left ventricle, small part of left auricle
Right ventricle, small part of left ventricle

tricks.label: C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive
tricks.text: Phrenic nerve roots are C3 to C5. The same nerve carries pericardial pain, which is why pericarditis can be felt at the shoulder.

tricks.label: Front to back: RV first, LA last
tricks.text: A knife through the sternum hits the RV. An enlarged LA pushes back on the esophagus (trouble swallowing) and can stretch the left recurrent laryngeal nerve (hoarseness).

tricks.label: Transverse sinus = finger behind the arteries
tricks.text: Slide a finger behind the aorta and pulmonary trunk and in front of the SVC. Surgeons pass a clamp or ligature through this sinus to stop arterial outflow during bypass.

highYield: Left atrial enlargement (for example from mitral stenosis) can cause dysphagia and hoarseness.
Cardiac tamponade: fluid in the pericardial sac compresses the heart; Beck triad is hypotension, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds.
Pericardial pain refers to the shoulder because of the phrenic nerve.
Phrenic nerve runs anterior to the lung root on the pericardium; vagus runs posterior to the lung root.
The fibrous pericardium does not stretch quickly, so even a small fast bleed can cause tamponade.
A stab wound just left of the sternum most likely enters the right ventricle.
pitfalls: The base of the heart is its posterior surface (mostly LA), and the apex points anteroinferiorly to the left.
Epicardium equals visceral serous pericardium; it is part of the heart wall.
Transverse sinus is behind the great arteries; oblique sinus is behind the left atrium.
The right border on a chest X-ray is the right atrium, while the left border is mostly the left ventricle.

summary: Where the four heart valves sit, how pressure differences open and close them, and how the valve events line up with pressures, volumes, heart sounds, and the ECG in one cardiac cycle. This is the foundation for every murmur and valve disease question.

points: Tricuspid valve (RA to RV): anterior, posterior, and septal cusps.
Mitral valve (LA to LV): anterior and posterior cusps.
Chordae tendineae tie AV cusps to papillary muscles; papillary muscles tighten in systole so cusps do not flip into the atria.
Pulmonary valve: anterior, right, and left cusps.
Aortic valve: right, left, and posterior cusps; right and left aortic sinuses give rise to the coronary arteries.
All four valves open and close passively, driven by pressure differences.
Aortic area: right 2nd intercostal space at the sternal border.
Pulmonic area: left 2nd intercostal space at the sternal border.
Tricuspid area: left lower sternal border.
Mitral area: apex, left 5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line.
Aortic valve opens when LV pressure rises above aortic pressure (about 80 mmHg).
Normal aortic pressure about 120/80 mmHg; pulmonary artery about 25/8 mmHg.
End-diastolic volume about 110 to 120 mL, stroke volume about 70 mL, end-systolic volume about 40 to 50 mL.
Ejection fraction = SV / EDV, normally about 55 to 70%.
Most ventricular filling is passive; atrial contraction adds about the last 20%.
Dicrotic notch (incisura) on the aortic pressure curve marks aortic valve closure.
a wave: right atrial contraction.
c wave: RV contraction bulges the closed tricuspid valve into the RA.
x descent: atrial relaxation and downward pull of the tricuspid ring during ejection.
v wave: RA fills against the closed tricuspid valve.
y descent: RA empties into the RV after the tricuspid valve opens.
Inspiration lowers chest pressure, raises venous return to the right heart, lengthens RV ejection, and delays P2.
Normal (physiologic) split widens on inspiration.

tricks.label: All Physicians Take Money
tricks.text: Listening areas in order from the right upper chest to the apex: Aortic, Pulmonic, Tricuspid, Mitral.

tricks.label: Kentucky and Tennessee
tricks.text: S3 follows S2 with the rhythm of Kentucky (S1, S2, S3). S4 comes before S1 with the rhythm of Tennessee (S4, S1, S2).

tricks.label: Valves are doors pushed by pressure
tricks.text: A valve opens when the pressure behind it is higher than the pressure in front of it, and shuts when that reverses. Find which pressure line is on top in a Wiggers diagram and you know the valve status.

highYield: Isovolumetric phases are the only times all four valves are closed.
Loss of the atrial kick in atrial fibrillation removes S4 and lowers filling in a stiff ventricle.
Fixed splitting of S2 points to an atrial septal defect.
Paradoxical splitting points to delayed LV emptying, such as aortic stenosis or left bundle branch block.
The c wave is the closed tricuspid valve bulging into the RA as the RV contracts; the x descent is atrial relaxation plus the tricuspid ring pulled down during ejection.
Papillary muscle rupture after MI lets mitral cusps prolapse and causes acute mitral regurgitation.
pitfalls: S1 marks the start of isovolumetric contraction, which comes before ejection; the aortic valve opens later.
Papillary muscles do not pull the AV valves open; they hold the cusps shut during systole.
S3 can be normal in a child or pregnant patient; the same sound in an older adult points to disease.
Wide split still varies with breathing; fixed split does not.

Volume falls to ESV during ejection

Isovolumetric relaxation with volume flat at ESV
Mitral opens where LV pressure drops below LA pressure, then rapid filling
P wave before atrial kick; QRS before isovolumetric contraction; T wave near end of ejection

summary: How an action potential in a ventricular muscle cell triggers calcium release and contraction, and how calcium handling sets the strength and speed of each beat. Expect questions on ion channels by phase, calcium-induced calcium release, and how sympathetic input raises contractility.

points: Resting potential is about -90 mV, held by inward rectifier K+ channels.
Upstroke comes from fast voltage-gated Na+ channels.
The plateau comes from L-type Ca2+ influx balanced by K+ efflux.
The action potential lasts about 0.2 to 0.3 s, far longer than in skeletal muscle.
The long refractory period lasts almost as long as contraction, so the heart cannot be tetanized.
The action potential spreads into T tubules and opens L-type Ca2+ channels (dihydropyridine receptors).
Entering Ca2+ opens ryanodine receptors (RyR2) on the SR: calcium-induced calcium release.
Ca2+ binds troponin C, tropomyosin moves, and myosin-binding sites on actin are exposed.
Cross-bridges cycle using ATP until Ca2+ falls.
Cardiac muscle needs extracellular Ca2+ to contract; skeletal muscle does not.
SERCA pumps most Ca2+ back into the SR.
Phospholamban brakes SERCA; when PKA phosphorylates phospholamban, the brake comes off.
The Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (3 Na+ in for 1 Ca2+ out) removes Ca2+ from the cell.
A sarcolemmal Ca2+-ATPase removes a smaller share.
Relaxation uses ATP, so ischemia impairs relaxation as well as contraction.
Every cell contracts with every beat, so force is graded by Ca2+ and sarcomere length, with no motor unit recruitment.
Sympathetic β1 stimulation raises cAMP and activates PKA.
PKA phosphorylates L-type Ca2+ channels (more Ca2+ in), phospholamban (faster SR uptake, bigger SR store), and troponin I (faster relaxation).
Stretch (Frank-Starling) improves filament overlap and raises troponin C sensitivity to Ca2+.
Blocking the Na+/K+-ATPase raises cell Na+, slows Ca2+ removal by the exchanger, and strengthens contraction (cardiac glycoside mechanism).
Heart muscle depends almost entirely on aerobic metabolism and burns mostly fatty acids at rest.
It extracts a large share of delivered O2 even at rest, so more demand must be met by more coronary flow.

rows: Motor neuron releases ACh at the neuromuscular junction
Action potential spreads from neighbor cells through gap junctions

tricks.label: Phase story: Na, K, Ca, K, rest
tricks.text: Phase 0 Na+ rushes in, phase 1 K+ starts out, phase 2 Ca2+ holds the plateau, phase 3 K+ pulls it down, phase 4 rests.

tricks.label: Phospholamban is a brake
tricks.text: Unphosphorylated phospholamban slows SERCA. PKA phosphorylation releases the brake, so Ca2+ is pumped back faster: quicker relaxation and a bigger store for the next beat.

tricks.label: Calcium is the volume knob
tricks.text: Anything that raises cytosolic Ca2+ during systole (β1 stimulation, slower Ca2+ removal) turns up force. Anything that lowers it turns force down.

highYield: Calcium-induced calcium release through RyR2 is the core of cardiac excitation-contraction coupling.
The plateau (phase 2) depends on L-type Ca2+ channels.
A refractory period nearly as long as contraction prevents tetany and lets the heart refill.
β1 stimulation raises contractility and speeds relaxation through PKA phosphorylation of L-type channels, phospholamban, and troponin I.
High extracellular K+ makes the resting potential less negative, inactivates some fast Na+ channels, and slows conduction.
Inhibiting the Na+/K+-ATPase raises intracellular Ca2+ through reduced Na+/Ca2+ exchange.
pitfalls: Ventricular myocytes use Na+ for the upstroke; SA and AV nodal cells use Ca2+ (covered in CV-7).
In skeletal muscle the DHPR is linked mechanically to RyR1; in cardiac muscle Ca2+ entry is the trigger.
Phosphorylating phospholamban speeds SERCA; it does not block it.
Calcium binds troponin C in both striated muscles; calmodulin is the smooth muscle partner.

l: Action potential travels down the T tubule
L-type Ca2+ channels open and Ca2+ enters
Ca2+ opens RyR2 and the SR releases more Ca2+
Ca2+ binds troponin C and tropomyosin shifts
Cross-bridge cycling shortens the sarcomere
SERCA pumps Ca2+ back into the SR (phospholamban regulates it)
Na+/Ca2+ exchanger moves Ca2+ out of the cell

dumps.p: Draw a ventricular myocyte action potential. Label phases 0 to 4, the voltage values, the ion moving in each phase, and the refractory period.
l: Resting about -90 mV in phase 4
Steep phase 0 from fast Na+ influx
Small notch in phase 1 from transient K+ efflux
Long plateau in phase 2 from L-type Ca2+ in and K+ out
Phase 3 repolarization from delayed rectifier K+
Effective refractory period spans most of the action potential

summary: What sets cardiac output from beat to beat: heart rate plus the three stroke volume controls (preload, afterload, contractility), and the reflexes that adjust them. Exam questions ask you to predict how a change shifts stroke volume, ejection fraction, or a pressure-volume loop.

points: Cardiac output (CO) = stroke volume (SV) x heart rate (HR); about 5 L/min in a resting adult.
Ejection fraction (EF) = SV / EDV.
Mean arterial pressure (MAP) = CO x total peripheral resistance.
MAP is about diastolic pressure plus one third of pulse pressure at resting heart rates.
Fick principle: CO = O2 consumption / (arterial O2 content minus venous O2 content).
Wall stress (Laplace) = pressure x radius / (2 x wall thickness).
Preload is ventricular stretch at end of diastole, best judged by end-diastolic volume.
Set mainly by venous return.
Frank-Starling: more filling gives a stronger beat and larger SV, so the heart pumps out what comes in.
Venous return rises with mean systemic filling pressure (about 7 mmHg) and falls as right atrial pressure rises.
Afterload is the wall stress the ventricle must overcome to eject.
For the LV it mostly tracks aortic pressure; it rises in hypertension and in aortic stenosis.
Higher afterload raises ESV and lowers SV.
Concentric hypertrophy thickens the wall and lowers wall stress back toward normal.
Contractility is force at a given preload and afterload; it rises with sympathetic β1 input and falls with ischemia, acidosis, and hypoxia.
Intrinsic SA node rate after autonomic blockade is about 100 bpm, so resting rate shows vagal tone.
Fast heart rates shorten diastole much more than systole, which cuts filling time and LV coronary flow.
Myocardial O2 demand rises with heart rate, contractility, and wall stress.
Carotid sinus baroreceptors signal through CN IX and respond to rises and falls in pressure.
Aortic arch baroreceptors signal through CN X, mainly to rises in pressure.
Both feed the nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla.
Falling pressure lowers baroreceptor firing, so sympathetic output rises (faster, stronger beats, vasoconstriction) and vagal output falls.
Atrial stretch speeds heart rate (Bainbridge reflex).

tricks.label: Preload is volume, afterload is pressure
tricks.text: Preload asks how full the ventricle is before it squeezes. Afterload asks how hard it must push to get blood out.

tricks.label: Read the loop by its corners
tricks.text: The lower right corner is EDV (preload). The upper left corner is ESV and aortic pressure (afterload). The loop width is SV. Move one corner and see what happens to the width.

tricks.label: Baroreceptor direction
tricks.text: Baroreceptors fire more when stretched. Low pressure means less firing, and the brain answers with more sympathetic and less vagal output.

highYield: SV depends on preload, afterload, and contractility; CO = SV x HR.
Normal EF is about 55 to 70%; it falls when contractility falls.
Raising afterload raises ESV and lowers SV.
Tachycardia shortens diastole and reduces LV coronary perfusion.
Carotid sinus uses CN IX; aortic arch uses CN X.
Concentric LV hypertrophy is the adaptation that lowers wall stress in pressure overload.
pitfalls: Increasing preload raises SV with little change in ESV; increasing contractility raises SV by lowering ESV.
Contractility is independent of preload; a stronger beat from more filling is the Frank-Starling effect.
The vagus has little direct effect on ventricular force even though it slows the heart a lot.
MAP equals diastolic plus one third of pulse pressure only at normal resting rates.

Carotid sinus afferents in CN IX

summary: Where the heart's conduction system lies, how pacemaker cells fire on their own, how the autonomic nervous system speeds or slows them, and how the ECG records the result. Questions ask you to link a wave or interval to a cardiac event and a lead group to the wall and artery it views.

points: SA node: right atrial wall near the SVC opening, at the top of the crista terminalis.
AV node: lower interatrial septum near the opening of the coronary sinus.
AV bundle (His) crosses the fibrous skeleton, the only normal electrical link from atria to ventricles.
Bundle splits into right and left bundle branches; the left has anterior and posterior fascicles.
Right bundle branch reaches the anterior papillary muscle through the moderator band.
Purkinje fibers spread the impulse through the subendocardium.
SA nodal artery comes from the RCA in about 60% of people.
AV nodal artery comes from the RCA in about 80% of people (right-dominant hearts).
No true resting potential; lowest point about -60 mV.
Phase 4: slow climb from the funny current (If, Na+ in through HCN channels), then T-type Ca2+.
Phase 0: slow upstroke from L-type Ca2+ channels once threshold (about -40 mV) is reached.
Phase 3: K+ efflux repolarizes. There is no phase 1 or 2.
The fastest pacemaker (normally the SA node) suppresses slower ones (overdrive suppression).
Norepinephrine on β1 receptors raises cAMP, increases If and Ca2+ currents, and steepens phase 4.
Acetylcholine on M2 receptors lowers cAMP and opens K+ channels, hyperpolarizes the cell, and flattens phase 4.
AV node delay (about 0.1 s) lets the atria finish filling the ventricles; sympathetic input shortens it and vagal input lengthens it.
Standard paper at 25 mm/s: small box 0.04 s, large box 0.20 s; 10 mm = 1 mV.
Heart rate is about 300 divided by the number of large boxes between R waves.
Depolarization moving toward a positive electrode gives an upward deflection.
Septum depolarizes first (left to right), then apex, then free walls from endocardium to epicardium; the base is last.
Repolarization runs epicardium to endocardium, so the T wave normally points the same way as the QRS.
Normal QRS axis is about -30° to +90°.
First degree: PR over 0.20 s, every P wave conducts.
Second degree Mobitz I (Wenckebach): PR lengthens beat by beat until a QRS is dropped; usually AV node.
Second degree Mobitz II: QRS dropped without PR lengthening; usually below the AV node and can progress.
Third degree: P waves and QRS complexes beat independently; an escape rhythm drives the ventricles.

charts.title: ECG waves and intervals
rows: Atrial depolarization plus AV nodal delay
Same direction as QRS in most leads
Shortens as heart rate rises; read as rate-corrected QTc

rows: Left circumflex (V5 and V6 may be LAD)

tricks.label: Park AT VENtura AVenue
tricks.text: Conduction speed from fastest to slowest: Purkinje, Atria, Ventricles, AV node.
Find an R wave on a thick line. Count the next thick lines as 300, 150, 100, 75, 60, 50. Where the next R wave lands is the approximate heart rate.

tricks.label: Leads II, III, aVF look at the floor
tricks.text: All three have their positive pole on the left leg, so they view the inferior wall, which usually gets its blood from the RCA.

highYield: The AV node is the slowest part of the conduction system; that delay lets the atria finish ventricular filling.
SA nodal artery from the RCA in about 60% and AV nodal artery from the RCA in about 80%, so inferior MI often causes bradycardia or AV block.
Phase 0 in nodal cells is Ca2+ driven, so Ca2+ channel blockade slows AV conduction.
Einthoven's law: lead II = lead I + lead III.
Lyme carditis classically causes third-degree AV block.
Mobitz II is more dangerous than Mobitz I because the block is usually below the AV node.
Prominent U waves suggest hypokalemia.
pitfalls: The PR interval is measured from the start of P to the start of QRS; the PR segment is only from the end of P.
Atrial repolarization has no visible wave because it is hidden in the QRS.
The T wave is upright even though repolarization is the opposite of depolarization, because it travels in the opposite direction (epicardium to endocardium).
Mobitz I has progressive PR lengthening; Mobitz II has a constant PR before the dropped beat.

Bundle of His through the fibrous skeleton
Right bundle branch through moderator band; left bundle with two fascicles
Purkinje fibers in subendocardium
Pacemaker phase 4 slow rise from If (HCN) then T-type Ca2+
Phase 0 slow upstroke from L-type Ca2+
Phase 3 K+ efflux; no plateau
